offence_severity: Life imprisonment/ fine under Section 302/498-A read with Section 34, Indian Penal Code
number_of_offences: Three offences/counts charged, two finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the dying declaration of the deceased as a truthful and reliable statement, even though it was not in question-answer form, and held that it may form the sole basis of conviction if subjected to close scrutiny and found to be truthful.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, including the eight-year-old daughter of the deceased, with caution, noting that the child's statement was potentially influenced by her living circumstances with the accused and that there was no eye-witness to the incident.

legal_representation.accused: Ms. Meenakshi Arora, Sr. Adv., Jasbir Singh Malik (For S. K. Sabharwal)
legal_representation.state: Roopansh Purohit, AAG, Ramesh Kumar, Ms. Naresh Bakshi and Daya Krishan Sharma

investigation_status: Case registered based on dying declaration, investigation completed, accused arraigned for trial

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted accused under Sections 302/498-A read with Section 34 IPC
appeal_history.high_court: Dismissed appeal, upheld trial court's judgment
appeal_history.supreme_court: Allowed appeal of Prem Kumar Gulati, acquitted him; upheld conviction of Mahender Singh

prosecution_argument: The prosecution established that the deceased was subjected to death at the instance and instigation of the husband, and that the husband poured kerosene oil and lit her on fire. The prosecution relied on the dying declaration and other evidence to establish the case against the husband.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the dying declaration was not in question-answer form and lacked corroboration, making it unreliable. They also highlighted the innocence of the accused Prem Kumar Gulati and his wife, noting they were found innocent during the investigation and were living separately.
legal_principle_applied: A truthful and reliable dying declaration may form the sole basis of conviction even though it is not corroborated, but the reliability of the declaration should be subjected to close scrutiny and the courts must be satisfied that the declaration is truthful.
precedent_relied_upon: Godhu & Anr. v. State of Rajasthan (1975) 3 SCC 241; K. Ramachandra Reddy V. Public Prosecutor (1976) 3 SCC 618; Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh (1973) 2 SCC 808; State of Karnataka v. Shariff (2003) 2 SCC 473; P Mani v. State of Tamil Nadu (2006) 3 SCC 161; Mohan Lal & Ors. v. State of Haryana (2007) 9 SCC 151
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed on the husband for his role in the death of the deceased, as the prosecution established his involvement in the commission of the offence.
